steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, latency, memory, context limits, and migration cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: ORBIT: Autoregressive Time Series Generation via Next Frequency-Band Prediction
summary: ORBIT replaces conventional time-series generative models (GANs, diffusion models, and standard autoregressive transformers) with a two-stage framework: a Frequency-Hierarchical VQ-VAE that decomposes latent representations into frequency bands with residual quantization, and a Frequency-Band Autoregressive Transformer that generates from low to high frequencies. The abstract claims state-of-the-art overall performance and superior inference efficiency compared with advanced baselines, but provides no quantitative factor in the abstract itself; assessing actual compute and memory costs requires consulting the full paper. The approach demands training both a custom VQ-VAE and a custom transformer on the reader's own time-series data, which adds implementation complexity and training time; it can fail if the reader lacks sufficient domain-specific training data, if the frequency decomposition does not match the characteristics of the target signals, or if the claimed efficiency gains do not materialize at the reader's data scale and sequence lengths.
rationale: ORBIT targets synthetic time-series generation rather than LLM inference or training efficiency, and adopting it requires implementing and training a custom two-component architecture whose benefits over simpler baselines are not quantified in the abstract, making it premature to adopt without validating the full paper's experimental setup against the reader's specific data constraints.
